studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops sorting a mixed fact set into three defensible groups within the unit “Explanatory Writing: Grouping, Precision, and Development.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's guided practice a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
Lay a flat sheet of paper across a gap between two books and it collapses under the weight of a single coin. Fold the same sheet into a row of narrow accordion pleats, lay it across the same gap, and it will hold a stack of coins. Nothing has been added. Only the shape has changed.

The explanation involves how a material resists bending. When a flat sheet bends downward, its top surface is squeezed and its bottom surface is stretched. The material closest to the middle of the sheet does almost nothing, because it is neither squeezed nor stretched. A flat sheet is thin, so nearly all of its material sits near that inactive middle.

Folding changes where the material sits. In a pleated sheet, some of the paper is lifted well above the center line and some is pushed well below it. Material located far from the center resists bending far more effectively than material near it. Engineers describe this using a quantity called the second moment of area, which increases sharply as material moves away from the middle.

This is why structural beams are shaped like the capital letter I. Most of the steel is concentrated in the top and bottom flanges, far from the center, while the thin vertical web in the middle mainly holds those flanges apart. An I-beam uses less steel than a solid rectangular bar of equal strength.

The same principle explains corrugated cardboard, ridged metal roofing, and the fluted edge of a pie crust. In each case a weak, thin material is made stiff not by adding more of it, but by moving what is already there farther from the center.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Why a Folded Sheet Beats a Flat One”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what sorting a mixed fact set into three defensible groups asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Why a Folded Sheet Beats a Flat One,” then answer: Apply sorting a mixed fact set into three defensible groups to paragraph 2, then check your decision against paragraph 4. What survives the check?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a checked application with an initial decision, evidence, and a revision if needed; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If sorting a mixed fact set into three defensible groups is not yet secure, return to “Why a Folded Sheet Beats a Flat One” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply sorting a mixed fact set into three defensible groups to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Why a Folded Sheet Beats a Flat One.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
